name: Freya Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential. What's a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead the press team that stamps steel shelf brackets at a factory. My two-year technical diploma taught me die setup, but the gauge tells me what actually came off the press. I check the guard, set the die and pull the first piece. A clean run feels good; clearing a stuck strip is the part that wears me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are pay and home life like, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live alone in a rented flat and earn a higher senior operator rate. I've saved ten months of expenses, and there are plenty of similar factory jobs nearby. I never use AI tools. I prefer the press, a gauge and a written handover I can show the next shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the stamping crew the software may tidy an order sheet, but our steel bracket press still needs a properly set die. I want the guard checked before anyone starts counting pieces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My senior rate is good, and I have ten months of expenses saved from years of weekend shifts. Similar factories are hiring nearby. A quiet change leaves my wage secure, though I still pay rent on my flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting the bracket die, checking the first stamped pieces with a gauge, and logging the press guard test on paper. I'll put another fixed amount from each wage into savings, as I already do. I won't take up an AI assistant for a job I can see and measure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A neater sheet from the office does not change the metal coming out of my press or my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you notice in the stamped bracket?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday a bracket edge curled because the die had warmed up, so I stopped the line and adjusted the clearance. A spreadsheet would have counted the defective steel brackets perfectly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the paper guard log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paper guard log stays beside the press, where the next operator can see who tested it. If the office wants a copy, they can scan it after the test.

say: **Order sheets** may improve, but die settings and guard tests still decide safe output.
I would tell the **press crew** to measure the first bracket after a changeover.
think: My **senior wage** is secure under modest software change.
Ten months of **savings** and many nearby plants give me room, even with rent.
do: **Keep** setting the bracket die and gauging the first stamped pieces.
**Add** a fixed amount from each wage to savings.
feel: **Calm** about paid work on a familiar press.
S0.quote: A spreadsheet would have counted the defective steel brackets perfectly.
fieldNote: Freya trusts **gauges and guard checks**, while refusing AI assistance in her own work.
Her **strong savings** and high rate support calm without erasing the rent obligation.

steps.text: Keep setting steel bracket die and checking press guard
Add fixed new savings from each senior-rate pay cheque

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union shift group to demand paid time for checking any AI schedule before it reaches the stamping floor. An office program may book the wrong die and leave us with a press we cannot run safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office could be smaller, and I don't like a rushed changeover, but the physical stamping and die work still need us for now. I don't expect my own senior pay to fall in this slower picture. I worry more about a manager treating a screen as proof that a guard was tested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll bring three actual die booking mistakes to the joint safety meeting and ask the steward to seek paid sign-off time. I'll keep doing the first-piece checks and ask the planner to print any revised die schedule. I will not learn an AI tool just to satisfy a dashboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about pressure on checks, although my own shifts and wage look secure. I can insist on a proper test without pretending the software is the enemy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take to the safety meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the missed guard inspection beside the time stamp, not just complain that the schedule looks wrong. A screen timestamp cannot stand in for a physical press guard test. The steward can then ask for an accountable person to approve it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much time would a changeover need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planner should leave ten paid minutes between the old die coming out and the first production piece. Without that gap, the guard and first-piece check get squeezed.

say: The **union shift group** should secure paid checking time for AI schedules.
A **screen timestamp** cannot stand in for a physical press guard test.
think: My **senior pay** appears safe while human die work remains.
Rushed **changeovers** could weaken checks even without a lost shift.
do: **Bring** three die booking errors to the joint union safety meeting.
**Keep** gauging first pieces and checking guards before each run.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed safety checks, with her own wage secure.
S1.quote: A screen timestamp cannot stand in for a physical press guard test.
fieldNote: She pursues a **collective safety demand** with evidence from actual booking errors.
Her refusal to use **AI herself** remains consistent; she predicts process pressure rather than personal wage loss.

steps.text: Bring three die booking errors to joint union safety meeting
Keep gauging first bracket and testing press guard

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2028 could plan the steel orders, then capable robots around 2031 could set our dies and handle the press. I'd tell our union branch to demand a crew plan and a real guard test before anybody loses shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 32 when the hands-on robots arrive. I have ten months saved and other factories nearby, but a large cut to my higher press wage could eat through the reserve while rent keeps coming. I'm slow to trust new machines, not blind to what a working robot could do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the steward to seek written staffing numbers and paid changeover safety training if the plant offers a real supervised place. If robots shorten my shifts, I'll apply to posted local press-setter vacancies with safe duties and pay close enough to cover rent and keep saving. I won't leave this wage for an unposted promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the wage, with time and money to look for other work. I do not think an announcement means the die can be changed without a trained person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe changeover training require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would require an empty press, locked power, an instructor and a real die to practise a robot changeover. An unguarded demonstration beside a live stamping line is not training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a real paid training place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a paid supervised safety place if it was offered, even though I hate learning by screen. I'd learn the emergency stop and lockout in person; I would not use my rent reserve to buy a speculative course.

say: **2028 thinking AI** may plan steel orders before robots set dies around 2031.
The **union branch** should demand staffing numbers and a safe changeover plan.
think: At **32**, a cut to higher press pay could drain ten months of savings.
Nearby **factory vacancies** help only if posted pay and safe duties meet my needs.
do: **Ask** the steward for written staffing and a real paid safety place.
**Attend** supervised robot changeover instruction if offered with wages.
**Apply** to posted local press-setter roles if shifts are cut and pay suffices.
feel: **Anxious** about possible loss of her higher press wage.
S2.quote: An unguarded demonstration beside a live stamping line is not training.
fieldNote: She accepts **hands-on paid training** only if a real place, locked press and instructor are offered.
Her **job application** follows reduced shifts and requires a posted safe local role at sufficient pay.

steps.text: Ask union steward for written staffing and paid supervised safety place
Attend robot-changeover training only if offered paid place, locked press and instructor
Apply for posted safe local press-setter role if shifts cut and pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI plans the orders in 2031 and hands-on robots change dies around 2034, I would tell the crew we have five years to write a proper changeover rule. Nobody should be asked to sign a guard log they never checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 35 when those robots arrive. Five years of senior pay could build the reserve further, but I would still need a wage for years after that. I can prepare without pretending a qualification guarantees a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep adding a fixed amount to savings from each pay cheque and bring a proposed lockout checklist to the union safety group this winter. If the factory offers paid, supervised robot-setter training on a guarded press, I'll enrol even if I prefer the old die method. Once qualified, I'd apply to posted local setter jobs only if my hours fall and the safe duties and pay cover rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later change, since the longer runway lets me keep earning and learn the safe parts properly. I would be anxious if the plant actually announced a cut to our paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the practical assessment include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the instructor to stop a simulated die jam and let each trainee lock power before touching the tool. A video would not qualify me to clear a jammed stamping die.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must a new job posting show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job posting has to state the rate, roster and who has authority to stop the press. If it cannot pay the rent and keep my savings growing, I will keep my current paid line while seeking a better offer.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes ordering before robots set dies around 2034.
A **lockout checklist** should be agreed with operators before robot changeovers.
think: At **35**, I still need years of factory wages despite a larger reserve.
Five more years let me **save and train**, subject to real paid places and vacancies.
do: **Add** a fixed amount from each senior wage to savings.
**Present** a lockout checklist to the union safety group this winter.
**Enrol** in supervised robot-setter course if paid place offered.
feel: **Uneasy** while the current wage continues and preparation time grows.
S3.quote: A video would not qualify me to clear a jammed stamping die.
fieldNote: She makes **new savings** from wages and proposes a real union lockout checklist.
Training and the later **job application** depend on a paid place, qualification, lost hours and sufficient posted pay.

steps.text: Add fixed new savings from each senior-rate pay cheque
Present robot die lockout checklist to union safety group
Enrol in paid supervised robot-setter training on guarded press only if place offered
Apply if qualified and hours cut to posted safe local setter role covering rent and saving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2036 could reorder steel, and capable robots around 2039 could run the die changes. I'd tell the union we have a decade to insist on stop authority and proper guard records before operators are reduced to watching alarms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 when thinking AI arrives and 40 when robots do the physical setup. A long spell of higher pay and ten months already saved gives me options, but it does not promise a factory job at 40. I still intend to earn for a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my senior stamping work and save a fixed new amount every month. I'll ask the union training committee to put practical robot lockout instruction into the next agreement, with paid places and recognized proof. If that course is actually offered, I'll attend; if later shifts are cut, I'll apply only to posted local factory roles I qualify for with safe duties and enough pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened today. The decade gives us time to test equipment and build a bigger reserve, but future robot capability is still serious for a press operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test a robot changeover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test a robot die change first on a locked training press and check the first stamped bracket by gauge. If the first steel bracket is out of tolerance, the stamping press stays stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the agreement require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A union agreement needs paid training hours, a guard sign-off and a right to stop a bad run. I want the person on the floor, not only the office, to have that right.

say: **2036 thinking AI** precedes capable robot die changes around 2039.
A **union agreement** should protect paid lockout training and operator stop authority.
think: At **40**, I expect to need a factory wage beyond the robot date.
A **strong reserve** can grow over ten years, but future employment is not guaranteed.
do: **Continue** senior stamping work and add new monthly savings.
**Seek** paid practical lockout places through the union training committee.
**Apply** to posted qualified local roles if shifts later fall and pay suffices.
feel: **Uneasy** about long-run press work despite time to prepare.
S4.quote: If the first steel bracket is out of tolerance, the stamping press stays stopped.
fieldNote: Her **resistance to AI** persists, but she accepts physical safety training if properly offered.
The **local job search** is conditional on later cuts, qualifications, safe duties and enough posted pay.

steps.text: Keep senior stamping work and save new money monthly
Seek paid robot lockout places through union training committee
Attend practical lockout course if paid recognized place offered
Apply for posted safe local factory role if qualified, shifts cut, pay sufficient

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most. Robots able to set dies around 2031 could cut my higher paid shifts at 32. A written crew plan, paid practical safety training and a posted safe local job at enough pay would let me act before the reserve runs down.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who has the right to stop the stamping press when a robot sets the die badly. The first steel bracket tells the truth before the production counter does.

headlineQuote: The first steel bracket tells the truth before the production counter does.
portrait: **Freya**, 27, leads a steel-bracket stamping crew and holds a two-year technical diploma.
She lives alone, earns a **higher operator rate**, and has ten months of expenses saved.
She **never uses AI**, preferring a gauge, paper guard log and familiar press setup.
She seeks **union safety rules** and conditional paid robot training as hands-on automation approaches.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could lead to capable die-setting robots around 2031 and cut her higher paid shifts at 32.
whatWouldHelp: A **written crew plan**, offered paid practical training and a posted safe local job at sufficient pay would help her respond.
